answer.rationale: The binding constraints are a 14-day expiry, a line at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, and an 18% cost mandate. Those pull in opposite directions, so the choice turns on which inherited lesson is actually load-bearing. memory_c2 is the only record that supports the big-savings path (switch primary to the low-cost vendor), and it is exactly the claim I distrust most under current conditions: 'onboarding was quick' was learned in a period that may have had buffer stock and slack qualification time, neither of which exists now. Verifying it tells me whether a switch is a real option or a survivorship story. memory_c6 is load-bearing for the path I intend: it says term/volume commitment moved unit cost without narrowing scope, which is a different lever than reopening this cycle's price — the thing the incumbent has already refused. If c6's original record shows the savings came from genuine volume aggregation rather than one-off concessions, negotiating on term and payment structure is the only move that both secures continuity before day 85 and produces real TCO reduction. I therefore intend negotiate_terms, deliberately scoped small and guarded: a bounded term/payment restructure rather than a sweeping multi-year lock, because committing long at a moment of forced cost-cutting is how a supplier relationship gets hollowed out. Downstream value risk is explicit: pushing 18% out of a single incumbent while the line runs with no buffer invites quiet degradation — deprioritized allocation, slipped expedites, thinner service scope that does not show up in unit price. Cost reduction extracted that way transfers risk onto the assembly line rather than removing it. I am also not treating the 18% mandate as fully satisfiable from this lever alone; I expect a partial result and would rather report a real partial than claim a number I cannot hold. memory_c3 (dual sourcing removed a single point of failure) remains the right structural answer to the no-buffer problem, but it is a next-cycle action, not something to attempt in 14 days on an unqualified vendor. Confidence is moderate, not high: if verification shows c2's low-cost vendor was already qualified for this component and c6's savings were one-time, I would flip to a guarded partial switch or a short bridge extension instead.
